title: Candidates, cost and ergonomics
goal: Which words get a stroke, which strokes are reserved first, every source of candidate outlines, the formula that ranks them, and how the ergonomic term scores finger shape.

blocks.x: Who counts as a word

`ranked_words` takes the frequency list's top 100,000 with a pronunciation, in plain lowercase (letters and apostrophes only). Two token kinds are dropped: frequency-list artifacts that claimed short strokes they could never use.

**Gold-only words come after them.** Every word Plover or Lapwing writes, and every word two or more of the other theories write (`Gold::vocabulary`), that the 100,000 cut or a missing pronunciation left out (*supercalifragilisticexpialidocious*, ranked 115,821, pronounced nowhere) is settled in the same pass, ranked after the rest, counted at least once said. A word with sounds takes the normal pool; one without has only its typable one-stroke gold outlines, with no faithful check (no sounds to check against). The solver trades strokes for them like any other word: [[supercalifragilisticexpialidocious|STPRAPBLG]] holds the stroke *suffrage* had; *suffrage* is [[suffrage|SUFRPBLG]]. Only one-stroke outlines can be borrowed: another theory's multi-stroke outline has no join keys. These words count toward neither the unplaced words nor the contested words the guards bound. Their backups are not in the solver's lexicon, so `solve --eval` shows a lower unweighted top-1 (about 72.9% of 40,314; the test set gained about 9,000 gold-only backups); the use-weighted figure is 92.6%.

items: **The bare letter "i".** The list spells the pronoun lowercase, so the letter would inherit the pronoun's count. The pronoun keeps [[I|EU]]; the letter is fingerspelled. `a` is the only single-letter word.

**Contraction tails** (`'s 'd 'll 're 'm 've 't 'n 'a`). The tokenizer splits "I've" into "i" + "'ve", so each tail would carry a whole contraction family's count, and struck alone would type the tail with its space. Their strokes go to real words: [[guess|TKPWES]], [[you'll|UL]], [[um|UPL]], [[tour|TUR]]. Clipped words real on their own (`'cause`, `'em`, `'til`) stay.

The candidate pool

`enumerate_candidates` is a pure function: a word in, every legal outline out, tagged with its source; no shared state. The pool is built across every core (`enumerate_in_parallel`) with a byte-identical result. No candidate is preferred by construction; the solver settles it on cost. Candidates with the same rendered text are deduplicated, keeping the cheaper.

blocks.x: A short form never takes a stroke the plain rules already give

items: A brevity step (and its first two star rungs) is dropped if some word's plain rules already give that text: every outline derivable by the rules stays that word's.

A short form landing on the starred stroke of a one-syllable rules stroke pays `STAR_SURCHARGE` (12,500, half a stroke) on top of its cost. A star on a one-syllable stroke means its sound-alike: [[dock|TKO*BG]] and [[sock|SO*BG]] carry the star, [[doc|TKOBG]] does not.
The surcharge is a price, not a ban: a short form that would otherwise cost a whole extra stroke, for a word much commoner than the sound-alike, still takes it: [[attack|TA*BG]] keeps its star.

blocks.x: The cost formula
`candidate_cost` depends on the outline alone, not the word, its frequency or other candidates. Every candidate from every source reduces to one number.

head: Tier
Weight
Why it ranks there
rows: A stroke costs 25 keys, one stroke holds at most 24: a one-stroke outline always beats any two-stroke one, so no word prefers a longer outline for itself.
Under 1,000 even for every key at once (`*` included, scores 928): only breaks ties between candidates with equal strokes and keys. The only tier that knows which keys.

Where frequency enters
Frequency is not in the formula. The solver multiplies a candidate's cost by how often the word is said (its frequency-corpus count), one level up:
edge_cost(word, candidate) = weight(word) x candidate_cost(candidate.outline)

Minimizing the sum of `edge_cost` over all words is the whole objective; `!build` reports the same metric as keys per word weighted by frequency. For one word, frequency does not change which of its candidates is best; it decides who wins when two words want the same text.
Why a stroke weighs 25 keys

25 is the smallest round number above the 24 keys one stroke can hold, which fixes the per-word order; only cross-word trades move. The weight is finite so that, once frequency is multiplied in, one extra stroke for a rare word is weighed against extra keys for a common one instead of always winning. Ergonomics: what costly means at the finger level

Two outlines can tie on strokes and keys yet feel different. [[TK]], one finger pressing both of its own rows, is easy. [[STWH]], four fingers alternating top and bottom, is not, though also one stroke and four keys. `src/ergonomics.rs` tells them apart. Every number traces to the keyboard geometry keymux presses or a finger-biomechanics measurement (Häger-Ross and Schieber, J Neurosci 2000).
Every key is a reach vector
Each key is a `(vertical, lateral)` reach, each axis 0 (the finger's own row) or 1 (one key away), checked key by key against the QWERTY layout keymux presses.

items: The right pinky's `D` and `Z` pair uses the stretch column.

The right index's `*` is struck via `H` (home, lateral) or `Y` (top, lateral). `*` folds into the right index's column as a wildcard: it fills whichever of `F` or `R` is unused, so `*` plus `F` costs no more than a same-finger double press.
Only these two digits reach a second position; the overload is priced by reach distance through its vector, not a flat tax.

blocks.x: Two measurements: the ring finger struggles most

Häger-Ross and Schieber measured two indices per finger. **Individuation (II)**: how independently a finger moves to its own target while its neighbors move to theirs; the right quantity for two active fingers (a transition). **Stationarity (SI)**: how still a finger stays while its neighbors move; the right quantity for a finger held out of the way between two active ones (a gap). On both, the ring finger is the least independent, not the pinky.

Self-paced, averaged across the paper's left and right hand columns, times 1000; the deficit from 1.0 is what counts. Ring's `TRANS` is about 4.5 times index's. Left-hand digit order: little, ring, middle, index; right: index, middle, ring, little.
The four terms a stroke is scored on

head: Term
What it measures
Formula
rows: Walking a hand's active fingers in order, charging for how far two neighbors' reach vectors differ.
`(dv^2 + dl^2) x (TRANS[i] + TRANS[j])` for each pair of consecutively active fingers; zero when both reach the same way.
With two or more fingers active on a hand, each one's distance from rest.
`(v + l) x TRANS[finger]`; zero below two active fingers, so a same-finger double stays free.
A finger skipped between two active neighbors on the same hand.
Flat cost per pinky key press, for leverage.
`PINKY_TAX` = 5 per press (`S-` on the left; `T`, `S`, `D`, `Z` on the right). Excludes the join key.

items: A same-finger double press is charged +1 in total and nothing else.
Squaring the per-axis difference makes transitions convex: two poorly coupled fingers each reaching further costs much more than twice a small reach.

The join key is excluded from every term: it appears in nearly every continuation stroke, so costing it would penalize "more than one stroke", not a real word choice. It sits on the left index finger's inner column (`T` and `G`), so its position changes no cost.

The star is the right index only (`Y` or `H`). `S-` is a tall key pressed by `A` (home) or `Q` (top); the model always prices it at `A`, where it is typed, and offers no cheaper `Q` alternative as it does for the star.

`PINKY_TAX` is a judgment call, not a measurement. It is below every other nonzero term (the smallest nonzero engagement cost is 56), so it only breaks ties between candidates differing in pinky presses.
